questions.stem: A $\text{25}$ $\text{m}$ ladder rests against a vertical wall with its foot $\text{15}$ $\text{m}$ from the wall. Build a right triangle, of any size, whose marked angle $\theta$ equals the angle between the ladder and the wall.

canonical_solution.text_md: Picture the ladder, the wall and the ground as a right triangle. The ladder is the hypotenuse (25 m), the side opposite the right angle and the longest side.
The angle $\theta$ the question wants is the one between the ladder and the WALL, at the top of the ladder. It is not the angle at the foot of the ladder.
Read the sides from that angle: the foot's distance from the wall (15 m) lies across from $\theta$, so it is the opposite side. The wall itself touches $\theta$, so it is the adjacent side.
The two sides we know are the opposite side and the hypotenuse, so the ratio is the sine: $\sin\theta = \frac{15}{25} = 0.6$.
Triangles with the same angle have the same ratio, whatever their size. Drag the legs until the sine reads 0.6: legs 3 and 4 (hypotenuse 5), legs 6 and 8, or the ladder's own 15 and 20 all work.
Check against the book's method: $\theta = \sin^{-1}(0.6) \approx 36.87^\circ$, the angle between the ladder and the wall.

questions.stem: A cone is scaled so that every length on it (the base radius, the height and the slant height) is multiplied by the same factor $k$. Every face scales by $k^{2}$, so the total surface area (base plus curved surface) is multiplied by $k^{2}$, whatever the measurements of the cone are.
The total surface area has to become $4$ times as large, so $k^{2} = 4$.
Take the positive root: $k = 2$. Drag $k$ to $2$, so the radius, the height and the slant height are all doubled.
